steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a formal verification methodology (UPEC-DIT) for proving that hardware executes operations data-obliviously. Motivate it from constant-time programming and microarchitectural timing side channels, say what we found, and end with a contribution list organized by section.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Hardware no longer trusted; microarchitectural side channels; need holistic countermeasures
- Constant-time / data-oblivious programming and its assumptions
- Oblivious HW primitives; little verification at microarchitectural level
- Optimizations undermining constant-time (survey, Augury)
- Our methodology and findings
- Contributions by section

But in order to fully meet the strict demands of security-critical applications, we need a holistic combination of several countermeasures that takes the entire system stack into account.

The most prominent SW paradigm that tries to mitigate microarchitectural timing side channels is data-oblivious programming, also called constant-time programming. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, the view of hardware (HW) as a root-of-trust has been badly damaged. A flood of new security vulnerabilities has put the focus again on microarchitectural side channels. Both the software (SW) and the HW communities have proposed many countermeasures against these new security gaps. But in order to fully meet the strict demands of security-critical applications, we need a holistic combination of several countermeasures that takes the entire system stack into account.

The most prominent SW paradigm that tries to mitigate microarchitectural timing side channels is data-oblivious programming, also called constant-time programming. It works by assuming that the timing and the resource usage of certain operations inside a processor do not depend on their input data. Constant-time programming is an actively studied discipline and the SW community has made many important contributions, including open-source libraries, domain-specific languages, verification tools and dedicated compilers. However the term "constant-time" can be misleading, because execution times do not need to be constant. A variable timing of operations is acceptable as long as it only depends on public information. For example, in constant-time programming the program itself counts as public information. With this assumption, consider a Read-After-Write (RAW) hazard that causes a stall in a pipelined processor. The change in instruction timing is legal, because it is based on the public sequence of instructions and not on the (potentially confidential) operands.

The data-oblivious subset of the instruction set of a processor is often called the set of oblivious HW primitives. More complex instructions, which could be insecure, are decomposed into these primitives so that the behavior is data-oblivious. A simple example is a processor that implements a multi-cycle multiplication. A common optimization in a HW multiplier checks whether one of the operands is zero, and if so it produces the result after a single cycle. This creates a timing that depends on the data, and a possible side channel if the operand contains confidential information. So instead of issuing a multiplication, constant-time programming would replace the multiply instruction by a sequence of primitive instructions like add and shift. But there is no guarantee that even these simple instructions are really oblivious HW primitives. Whether an instruction fulfills the criterion of data-independent timing or not can vary between the implemented microarchitectures. Still, there is only little research on how to verify these assumptions at the microarchitectural level.

It gets worse: a recent survey pointed out seven classes of microarchitectural optimizations that all undermine the constant-time paradigm. Exploiting some of them in commodity processors may seem unrealistic, but an attack called Augury showed that this threat is not just theoretical. That work shows the security implication of one of these optimizations, data memory-dependent prefetchers, which are present in modern Apple processors. With more and more of these advanced optimizations being implemented, the question is how we can restore the trust in HW.

For this, we propose a new methodology for proving data-oblivious execution of HW operations using standard formal property checking techniques. For processors, the approach certifies a set of trusted HW primitives for data-oblivious programming. Our results show that even simple instructions like a logical shift can have an unexpected timing variability. We also found a potential timing vulnerability, which could be prevented, in the Ibex RISC-V core, which is extensively verified. We also extend the approach to out-of-order cores and show it is feasible and scalable with an experiment on the BOOM.

The contributions of this paper are:

- Sec. II – We give a comprehensive overview of related approaches that try to ensure data-obliviousness based on an analysis at the HW level.

- Sec. III – We introduce a definition of data-oblivious execution at the microarchitectural level and formalize it as a 2-safety property over infinite traces. Most HW designs are not built for data-obliviousness, so we also introduce a weaker notion, input-constrained data-obliviousness, for general designs. To make these properties verifiable in practice, we show how the definitions over infinite traces can be transformed into inductive properties that only span a single clock cycle.

- Sec. IV – We propose a formal verification methodology called Unique Program Execution Checking for Data-Independent Timing (UPEC-DIT) that can exhaustively detect any violation of data-obliviousness at the HW level. It is based on standard formal property languages, so it can easily be integrated into existing formal verification flows. Applied to processor implementations, UPEC-DIT can qualify the instructions of a microarchitectural ISA implementation with respect to data-obliviousness. These data-oblivious instructions are HW primitives for countermeasures like constant-time programming, so they can serve as a HW root-of-trust for the higher levels of the system stack.

- Sec. V – We present several optimization techniques, like black-boxing, proofs over an unrolled model and cone-of-influence reduction, which can further increase the scalability and usability of the methodology.

- Sec. VI – We show the feasibility of our approach with case studies on several open-source RTL designs. Besides several HW accelerators and in-order processors, our experiments also include the BOOM, a superscalar RISC-V processor with FP support, a deep 10-stage pipeline and out-of-order execution.

To make these properties verifiable in practice, we show how the definitions over infinite traces can be transformed into inductive properties that span only a single clock cycle.

- Sec. IV – We propose a formal verification methodology, called Unique Program Execution Checking for Data-Independent Timing (UPEC-DIT) [17], that can exhaustively detect any violation of data-obliviousness at the HW level. The methodology is based on standard formal property languages and can therefore be easily integrated into existing formal verification flows. When applied to processor implementations, UPEC-DIT can be used to qualify the instructions of a microarchitectural ISA implementation regarding their data-obliviousness. These data-oblivious instructions constitute HW primitives for countermeasures such as constant-time programming and can thus serve as a HW root-of-trust for the higher levels of the system stack.

- Sec. V – We present several optimization techniques, such as black-boxing, proofs over an unrolled model, and cone-of-influence reduction, which further increase the scalability and usability of the proposed methodology.

- Sec. VI – We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach through case studies on multiple open-source RTL designs. Besides several HW accelerators and in-order processors, our experiments also cover the BOOM [21], a superscalar RISC-V processor with FP support, a deep 10-stage pipeline and out-of-order execution.
